page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Definition
lines: Commensalism is an interaction between two
different species in which one species is
benefited and the other is neither benefited
steps.why: The definition is fixed by the SECOND species, not the first: the whole answer turns on the words neither benefited nor harmed, which separate commensalism from mutualism and from parasitism.
common_mistakes: Writing that the other species is harmed. That is parasitism.
Writing that both are benefited. That is mutualism.
steps.memory_tip: Count the gains: commensalism has one gain and one zero.
steps.margin_note: One sentence. The words neither benefited nor harmed must appear.

steps.label: Example

lines.text: One species gains, the other is unaffected

lines: Ex: barnacles growing on the back of a whale.
The barnacles get a place to live and food
The whale is not affected by them.
steps.why: The example must be explained in the same terms as the definition, so the answer states what one partner gains and then states plainly that the other is unaffected.
common_mistakes: Naming the example without saying who gains what. The explanation carries the mark.
Choosing bees and flowers as the example. Both gain there, so that is mutualism.
steps.memory_tip: Barnacle on the whale: the barnacle gets a free ride, the whale notices nothing.
steps.margin_note: Name the example, then one line on the gain and one on the unaffected partner.

insider_note: The three interaction terms are marked as a set, so the safest answer says in words what happens to BOTH partners, not just to the one that gains.
